# reproduce agent enrollment + host authorization (follow-up to #797) ## Context This document builds on the `reproduce` restructuring plan agreed in #797 (Phases 1 and 2 completed in #812 and #813) and the `reproduce-windows` implementation planned for Phase 3. It defines **Phase 4 and beyond** to address two requirements: 1. **Automatic per-endpoint mTLS identity issuance and rotation** — hundreds to thousands of `reproduce-*` instances must each connect to Giganto with a unique client certificate, with automatic scheduled rotation. 2. **Per-host authorization** — each customer or environment has a limit on how many hosts it is allowed to operate; when the grant expires or is suspended, that host's connection to Giganto must be blocked immediately. This is a **design agreement document**, not an implementation plan. Once agreed, it will be split into concrete issues across the affected repositories (reproduce, aice-web-next, aimer-web, bootroot, giganto, giganto-client), and this discussion will continue to serve as the **link hub**. > **Scope boundary**: This work is **not a license management system**. Business concerns such as product sales, subscriptions, and billing are explicitly out of scope. We only define the technical permission for "is this host allowed to send data to Giganto". Throughout this document and the resulting artifacts we deliberately avoid the word "license" and use **"host authorization"** instead. When the organization eventually introduces a full license or subscription system, it will sit *above* the mechanisms defined here. > **Revision history**: This document has gone through ten rounds of structured review. Major changes accumulated so far: > > *Round 1 — initial design hardening* > > - New **"Enrollment trust model"** section with two-factor binding (MDM fingerprint or out-of-band nonce). Bundle TTL tightened to 15 minutes; re-download disabled by default. > - New **"Data governance"** section: field minimization, per-tenant redaction, retention, DSR handling, region pinning. PIPA / GDPR / CCPA / CRA framing. > - **Internet-facing `bootroot-http01-responder` is deployed as a separate instance from v1** (no shared process with the internal-services responder). Closed-network deployments may still use the single dual-mode topology. > - The authorization webhook uses **mTLS plus HMAC** (defense in depth), not HMAC alone. > - **Windows Cert Store** (`WindowsCertStore`) is a v1 key-storage option alongside PEM, not a v2 deferral. > - Phase 4a split into four sub-phases (4a-1 through 4a-4) for incremental review. > - Interface contracts (webhook JSON, `HOST_DENIED` wire format, `activation.json` schema) moved to **versioned spec files** in each affected repo. > - **Staged CA trust** added as a v2 roadmap item for zero-downtime CA rotation. > > *Round 2 — contract precision and scope honesty* > > - **Internal contradiction fixed**: `E3` and `C5` now agree. `host.expected_fingerprint` (Path A authentication factor, set at issuance time) and `host.observed_fingerprint` (drift-detection record, set on first enrollment) are explicitly distinct. > - **Wire format defined**: the second factor (Path A fingerprint or Path B nonce) is carried inside the CSR through **custom X.509 extensions under a private OID arc**, stripped by the step-ca template before signing, and read by the authorizing webhook from the parsed CSR. Exact OIDs and encoding live in `reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md` and the corresponding portal spec files. > - **Path A claim corrected**: replaced "defeats bundle theft entirely" with "raises the bar significantly". `MachineGuid` / `/etc/machine-id` / `IOPlatformUUID` are *readable values*, not cryptographic attestations. Hardware-rooted attestation via `device-attest-01` + TPM / Secure Enclave is added as an explicit v2 candidate. > - **DSR v1 hardened** with five built-in safety guards: exact match only, field whitelist, two-stage preview/execute, soft delete with 30-day grace period, and signed export archives with download audit. > - **Metadata centralization acknowledged**: the region-pinning section now explicitly distinguishes the **event data path** (region-pinned in v1) from the **portal metadata path** (centralized in v1, with field-level minimization, audit-log scrubbing, and contractual disclosure as the v1 mitigations). **Regional portal database shards** added as an explicit v2 candidate. > > *Round 3 — contract consistency and compliance posture* > > - **Webhook auth contract unified**: all references to `POST /api/authz/host` — the portal API section, the authorization webhook sequence diagram, the aimer-web section, and the step-ca provisioner description — now consistently state **mTLS plus HMAC** as the required authentication. > - **Path B fingerprint gap closed**: the wire format now specifies that the agent **always** includes its host fingerprint (OID `.1.1`) in the CSR regardless of which trust path is used. For Path A it is an authentication factor; for Path B it is recorded as `observed_fingerprint` for forensics. The per-OID role table is updated accordingly. > - **Naming inconsistency fixed**: all references to the nonce column now use `host.expected_nonce_hash` (not `expected_nonce`). > - **DSR default changed from soft delete to hard delete**: to align with GDPR Art. 17 ("without undue delay") and PIPA Art. 21 ("without delay"), DSR deletions now perform an immediate hard delete by default. A time-delayed quarantine mode is available only when the operator has activated a legal-hold or incident-recovery policy override, with the justification recorded in the audit log. > > *Round 4 — write-semantics precision* > > - **`observed_fingerprint` made set-once**: the column is now written only on the first successful enrollment (when null) and is immutable thereafter. Subsequent renewals log the current fingerprint as an `enrollment.renewal_fingerprint` audit event instead of overwriting the forensic baseline. This prevents failed attempts from polluting the value and preserves the original enrollment record for forensics. > > *Round 5 — enrollment confirmation lifecycle* > > - **Two-phase enrollment model**: webhook `{"allow": true}` is now explicitly Phase 1 (authorization only, no state mutation). Phase 2 (confirmation) fires when Giganto reports the first connection with a previously unseen cert serial, and atomically commits `cert_serial`, `observed_fingerprint`, nonce consumption, and `status = Active`. This closes the gap where a download failure after webhook allow could consume one-time credentials and lock out Path B retries. > - **Retry-safe webhook logic** for Path B: since Phase 1 does not consume the nonce, a retried finalize simply re-verifies against the still-present `expected_nonce_hash`. No special-case bypass is needed. *(Note: the initial version of this bullet described a `nonce null + cert_serial null` bypass path; Round 6 corrected this to reflect that the nonce is never consumed at webhook time.)* > - **Enrollment confirmation via Giganto GraphQL subscription**: instead of Giganto pushing HTTP to the portal, Giganto exposes a `sensorConnected` subscription and the portal subscribes over the existing mTLS GraphQL WebSocket. No new outbound networking in Giganto. A `connectedSensors` query allows catch-up after subscription drops. > - **Audit event list completed**: `enrollment.confirmed` and `enrollment.renewal_fingerprint` added to the audit event catalog. > > *Round 6 — two-phase propagation cleanup* > > - **OID role table updated**: both OIDs now explicitly state *which phase* each action belongs to. Fingerprint recording and nonce consumption happen in Phase 2, not at webhook time. > - **Retry-safe logic rewritten**: the previous formulation implied the webhook consumed the nonce and then detected the consumed state on retry. Corrected to reflect that Phase 1 never consumes the nonce — retries simply re-verify against the still-present `expected_nonce_hash`. > - **Authorization webhook diagram fixed**: portal status check changed from `host.status = Active?` to `host.status in {Enrolling, Active}?` so that initial enrollments pass validation. > - **E5 rewritten**: previously conflated "no bundle at startup" with "enrollment failure". Now distinguishes three stages: no valid bundle → `PendingActivation`; transient enrollment failure → retries in `Enrolling`; non-transient failure → `Suspended`. > > *Round 7 — stale retry-bypass cleanup* > > - **Revision history Round 5 bullet and edge-case table**: removed the obsolete "`nonce null + cert_serial null` → allow without nonce" bypass description that Round 6 had already corrected in the main body. Both now state that Phase 1 never consumes the nonce, so retries simply re-verify normally. > > *Round 8 — operational security hardening* > > - **Audit log redaction of secret material**: the CSR body and its custom-extension values (nonce, fingerprint) must never be logged in plaintext. Audit entries record only a truncated hash of the fingerprint, a `nonce_present` boolean, and the decision. This is a MUST-level spec requirement. > - **Pending enrollment lease**: the webhook now sets a pending lease when it returns `allow`, preventing concurrent ACME flows from producing duplicate certificates for the same host identity. *(Note: Round 9 later refined this to a CSR-public-key-hash-scoped lease with ACME-order-lifetime timeout, and Round 10 corrected a stale "24 hours" reference. The current design uses `pending_issuance_key_hash TEXT` + `pending_since`, not a simple boolean.)* > - **Portal availability claim corrected**: the previous "independent from portal availability" statement was wrong — cert renewal requires the authorization webhook, making the portal a hard dependency. Replaced with "partial independence" that honestly describes the data-plane independence (agent ↔ Giganto) and the control-plane dependency (renewal ↔ portal). Portal HA is now an explicit operational requirement. A signed authorization lease for offline renewal is added as a v2 candidate. > - **Suspended recovery path clarified**: removed the fictitious "portal reactivation → next renewal window" recovery option. `Suspended` is now defined as recoverable **only** through new bundle injection. The agent has no active timers or network loops in this state and cannot self-recover. > - **MSI bundle delivery clarified**: the MSI property carries a **file path** to the bundle, never the bundle content itself. Passing raw JSON on the command line would expose EAB and HMAC secrets in installer logs, Sysmon events, and MDM logs. > - **Cross-repo conformance test suite** added to Phase 4a-4: shared fixtures that exercise contract boundaries (webhook JSON, `HOST_DENIED` wire format, CSR OIDs, enrollment confirmation) run in CI for each repo. > - **`ActivationBundle.giganto_addr`** changed from `SocketAddr` to `String` (hostname:port) to align with the DNS-based endpoint model used throughout the design. > > *Round 9 — lease scoping, renewal safety, and status enum* > > - **Enrollment lease redesigned**: the lease is now scoped to the **CSR public key hash** (not the host as a whole) and **only applies during initial enrollment** (`host.status = Enrolling`). Renewals (`host.status = Active`) are exempt — a lease on renewals would cause service outages when a retry is blocked while the cert approaches expiry. Idempotent retries (same key hash) pass through the lease; only a different key hash is blocked. Lease timeout matches the **ACME order lifetime** (1–4h), not the cert lifetime (24h). Schema columns changed from `pending_issuance BOOLEAN` to `pending_issuance_key_hash TEXT`. > - **`host.status` enum unified**: both portal schemas now explicitly list `Pending | Enrolling | Active | Suspended | Revoked` in the column comment. Previously `Enrolling` was used by the webhook and Phase 2 logic but was missing from the schema definition, risking divergent implementations. > > *Round 10 — stale text cleanup* > > - **Lease timeout**: one remaining paragraph still said "24 hours"; corrected to "ACME order lifetime (typically 1–4 hours)". > - **Renewal nonce reference removed**: the renewal section previously referenced "retry against the still-valid `expected_nonce_hash`", which is self-contradictory because the nonce was already consumed at Phase 2. Replaced with a clear statement that nonce verification is not involved in renewals. ## End-to-end scenario (from the user's perspective) Deploying a Windows endpoint at a closed-network customer site via aice-web-next: 1. The customer admin signs in to their on-premises aice-web-next. 2. They select "Add host" in the UI, pick a target customer (or environment + customer in aimer-web), and download an activation bundle (`activation.json`) together with the MSI. 3. On the Windows PC, the admin runs the MSI, supplies the activation bundle, and confirms the Sysmon installation prompt. The installer then registers the reproduce-windows service. 4. On first service start, the agent performs the enrollment protocol and receives a short-lived client certificate from step-ca. 5. It begins collecting Sysmon events and streaming them to Giganto. 6. After 16 hours (2/3 of the cert lifetime) the agent renews automatically; this repeats for the life of the host. 7. When the admin suspends the host in the portal, Giganto blocks it within seconds and sends an authoritative denial to the agent; on receiving that denial the agent self-suspends (stops collecting and stops sending); step-ca then refuses the next renewal, and the current cert expires naturally shortly after. Internet customers use aimer-web with the same flow. Linux and macOS follow the same logic with different packaging. --- ## Principles - **Reuse existing organizational standards.** Keep bootroot (step-ca + OpenBao + ACME) as the CA foundation, keep aice-web-next and aimer-web as the authentication and authorization authority, and keep Giganto as the data receiver. No new CA, no new authentication stack. - **Separate mTLS authentication from host authorization.** Certificates prove *who the host is*; portal state decides *whether it is allowed to send data*. These two responsibilities must never be conflated. - **Common library first.** The three OS binaries (reproduce-windows, reproduce-linux, reproduce-macos) sit on top of common enrollment, keystore, and state-machine traits in `src/lib.rs`. Platform code is a thin adapter layer. - **Portals are OS-agnostic.** The enrollment and renewal endpoints and the `activation.json` format are OS-independent. - **Linux as the reference implementation.** While the Windows SSL.com EV certificate is being provisioned, Windows platform-specific work proceeds in parallel so that no wall-clock time is wasted. - **Environment separation** (consistent with [bootroot ARCHITECTURE.md §6.2](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#62-environment-separation)). Closed-network customers use a customer-operated step-ca; internet customers use a company-operated step-ca. CA keys and trust roots are never shared across environments. - **Short-lived certificates plus an explicit deny list.** Certificates are issued for 24 hours so that a compromised cert is usable for at most 24 hours, and when immediate blocking is required, Giganto's deny list takes effect within seconds. No CRL, no OCSP. - **Reuse ACME.** No custom enrollment protocol; use ACME with EAB. Extend bootroot's `bootroot-http01-responder` pattern to the endpoint use case. - **Respect the scope boundary.** This is a host authorization gate, not a license or subscription system. Billing, sales, renewal notifications, and similar concerns are out of scope. - **Treat the activation bundle as a high-value secret.** A leaked bundle must not by itself be enough to obtain a valid certificate. Enrollment pins the bundle to a specific host through a pre-registered fingerprint or a one-time nonce verified by the portal out-of-band. - **Minimize and govern collected data.** Endpoint telemetry from Sysmon, Falco, and osquery often carries personal data (usernames, paths, command lines, URLs). Field minimization, redaction, per-tenant retention, and data-subject request handling are first-class requirements of this design, not afterthoughts. --- ## System components ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Portal["Portal layer (authority)"] direction LR AWN["aice-web-next
(closed-net UI)"] AMW["aimer-web
(internet UI)"] end subgraph PKI["PKI infrastructure (bootroot)"] direction LR StepCA["step-ca
• internal provisioner
• endpoints provisioner (new)"] OpenBao["OpenBao
• master HMAC
• per-host HMAC store"] Responder["bootroot-http01-responder
(extended with scoped mode)"] end subgraph Endpoints["Endpoint layer (reproduce-*)"] direction LR RW["reproduce-windows
Sysmon · Win Service · MSI (WiX)"] RL["reproduce-linux
Falco/osquery · systemd · .deb"] RM["reproduce-macos
osquery · launchd · pkg"] end Giganto["Giganto
• Verify SAN ↔ agent_name
• Deny list + admin API"] Portal -. "admin API" .-> PKI Portal -. "deny list API" .-> Giganto Endpoints -. "ACME + HTTP-01" .-> PKI Endpoints == "mTLS (with issued cert)" ==> Giganto ``` Portal responsibilities: user authentication (existing), host authorization (new `host` table with `max_hosts`), activation bundle issuance, EAB and HMAC entry provisioning, re-checking authorization on every renewal, and pushing cert serials to the Giganto deny list on suspension. --- ## Portal binding and runtime communication boundary This design cleanly separates *which portal governs which agent* from *who the agent actually talks to at runtime*. This boundary is how the architecture enforces its trust zone principles. ### 1. Portal binding is permanent Once a `reproduce-*` instance is enrolled through a specific portal, it is **permanently bound** to the **step-ca + responder + Giganto** infrastructure operated by that portal. Cross-portal migration is not supported in v1. The rationale comes from [bootroot `ARCHITECTURE.md` §6.2 "Environment Separation"](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#62-environment-separation): | Environment | CA operator | Trust boundary | |---|---|---| | Closed network | customer-operated step-ca | trusted only within that closed network | | Internet | company-operated step-ca | trusted only within the internet environment | The two step-ca root certificates are **not present in each other's trust store**. As a result: - An agent enrolled through aice-web-next holds a cert signed by that closed network's step-ca, and aimer-web's Giganto will reject it during the handshake. - The reverse is equally true. - **The only way to change portals is a full reinstall**: delete the existing key and cert, inject a new `activation.json`, and re-enroll. Because portal migration is rare and automatic migration would entail a CA trust swap combined with a core key swap, the implementation and operational cost is not justified for v1. **v2 roadmap — staged CA trust**: for fleets in the thousands, full reinstall is operationally painful when the underlying concern is "rotate the CA key without disrupting data collection". The planned v2 mechanism is *staged CA trust*: Giganto temporarily trusts both the old and the new root during a transition window, agents re-enroll through the normal renewal path (which naturally picks up the new CA via `activation.json` refresh), and the old root is retired once all hosts have migrated. This does not change the "portal binding is permanent" principle — a host is still bound to a single portal — but it removes full reinstall as the only CA-rotation path. ### 2. Runtime communication boundary — the agent never talks to the portal directly After the initial `activation.json` download, the `reproduce-*` binary **makes no runtime network connection to the `aice-web-next` or `aimer-web` domain**. At runtime the agent only talks to **step-ca + responder + Giganto**: | Endpoint | When | Purpose | |---|---|---| | **step-ca directory** | Initial enrollment and every renewal (at 2/3 of the cert lifetime) | ACME `newAccount` (with EAB), `newOrder`, `finalize`, fetch cert | | **HTTP-01 responder** | On each ACME challenge | Register the validation token with scoped HMAC authentication | | **Giganto** | Continuously, starting immediately after installation | mTLS event data stream | The portal (`aice-web-next` or `aimer-web`) only appears in two paths: - **Initial provisioning**: the admin uses a browser to download the activation bundle and the agent binary, then ships them to the target host via USB, GPO, MDM, or a similar channel. The agent process itself never contacts the portal. - **Administrative actions**: the admin clicks "suspend host" in the portal UI, the portal calls the **step-ca admin API and the Giganto admin API**, and the agent **indirectly** observes the result (the next renewal is denied, a deny list entry blocks the connection, a `HOST_DENIED` response is returned). Practical benefits of this separation: 1. **Partial independence from portal availability.** If the portal goes down, agents **that already hold a valid cert** continue to collect and send data to Giganto normally — the data plane (agent ↔ Giganto) has no portal dependency. However, **cert renewal requires the portal** because step-ca calls the authorization webhook on every issuance. A portal outage therefore blocks new enrollments, admin actions, **and renewals**. The natural grace window is the remaining cert lifetime (up to 8 hours if renewal triggers at the 2/3 mark of a 24-hour cert). If the portal recovers within that window, the agent's backoff retry succeeds and no data is lost. Portal HA (high availability) deployment is therefore an operational requirement for environments that cannot tolerate an 8-hour renewal blackout. A v2 candidate — a **signed authorization lease** that step-ca can validate locally without calling the webhook — would allow renewals to proceed during brief portal outages, but is out of scope for v1. 2. **Minimal protocol surface.** The agent only needs to speak ACME (a standard) and giganto-client (already in use). With no custom portal protocol, the version-compatibility burden and the attack surface both stay small. 3. **Portal releases are independent from agent releases.** A portal code change cannot break agent compatibility, and vice versa. 4. **Clean audit boundary.** The three endpoints the agent talks to are all bootroot infrastructure (step-ca, responder) or Giganto, each with its own audit log. The portal audit log captures "admin intent"; the infrastructure audit logs capture "actual enforcement". **Implementation note — new outbound connections required in both portals:** While agents never talk to the portal at runtime, the **portals themselves** need several new outbound connections that do not exist today: | Connection | Purpose | Current state | What to add | |---|---|---|---| | Portal → **Giganto GraphQL** (subscription) | Subscribe to `sensorConnected` for Phase 2 enrollment confirmation | **Does not exist.** aice-web-next only connects to review-web's GraphQL; aimer-web does not connect to Giganto at all | New env var (`GIGANTO_GRAPHQL_ENDPOINT`), new mTLS agent, **WebSocket transport** (`graphql-ws` or equivalent) for subscription support. `graphql-request` (currently used by aice-web-next) is HTTP-only and cannot do subscriptions | | Portal → **Giganto GraphQL** (mutation) | Push deny list entries | Same as above | Same client, using the mutation transport | | Portal → **step-ca admin API** | Create/delete per-host EAB credentials | **Does not exist** in either portal | New HTTP client with admin credentials (from OpenBao) | | Portal → **bootroot responder admin API** | Create/delete per-host scoped HMAC entries | **Does not exist** in either portal | New HTTP client with mTLS or AppRole auth | These connections are prerequisites for AW-3 through AW-6 (aice-web-next: host creation, webhook, subscription, and suspend/deny-list push) and AM-2 through AM-4 (aimer-web). In the implementation plan ([patio#618](https://github.com/orgs/aicers/discussions/618)), the outbound infrastructure setup is AW-2 (aice-web-next) and AM-2 (aimer-web), producing shared utility modules (e.g. `lib/giganto-client.ts`, `lib/step-ca-admin.ts`, `lib/responder-admin.ts`) that subsequent steps consume. ### 3. Per-environment concrete example **Closed-network customer (aice-web-next)** ``` URLs embedded in activation.json (all inside the customer's closed network) step_ca.directory = https://step-ca.customer-abc.local/acme/endpoints/directory responder.url = https://responder.customer-abc.local giganto.addr = giganto.customer-abc.local:38370 Runtime network connections: reproduce-windows → https://step-ca.customer-abc.local (ACME) reproduce-windows → https://responder.customer-abc.local (HTTP-01 token) reproduce-windows → giganto.customer-abc.local:38370 (mTLS data stream) Provisioning-time network connections (from admin browser, not from agent): admin browser → https://aice-web-next.customer-abc.local (add host, download MSI and bundle) reproduce-windows never connects to aice-web-next.customer-abc.local. ``` **Internet customer (aimer-web)** ``` URLs embedded in activation.json (all in company-operated infrastructure) step_ca.directory = https://step-ca.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com/acme/endpoints/directory responder.url = https://responder.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com giganto.addr = giganto.aimer.aicers.com:38370 Runtime network connections: reproduce-windows → https://step-ca.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com (ACME) reproduce-windows → https://responder.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com (HTTP-01 token) reproduce-windows → giganto.aimer.aicers.com:38370 (mTLS data stream) Provisioning-time network connections: admin browser → https://aimer.aicers.com (add host, download MSI and bundle) reproduce-windows never connects to aimer.aicers.com. ``` In both cases the agent's runtime peers fall into the same three categories (step-ca, responder, Giganto), all sitting inside a single environment's trust zone. ### 4. Cases that require re-establishing the portal binding (reference) In the following scenarios the portal binding must be reset. In v1 all of them are handled by **reinstallation**: - The customer decommissions its closed-network AICE and moves to different internal infrastructure. - The organization rebuilds a customer-operated step-ca (CA key rotation). - An agent is physically moved to a different customer environment. - The existing cert or key is damaged, or a compromise is suspected. Reinstall procedure: stop the agent service, delete the existing cert, key, and bundle files, issue and download a new activation bundle from the portal, inject it, and restart the service. The state machine then goes `PendingActivation → Enrolling → Running`. This procedure begins from the `Suspended` or `Stopped` state. --- ## Decision summary ### A block — technical and organizational decisions | # | Item | Decision | |---|---|---| | A1 | ACME challenge | **HTTP-01 + reuse of bootroot's shared responder**. `device-attest-01` lacks an end-to-end flow in open-source step-ca, and TPM dependence restricts deployment coverage | | A2 | Linux distribution scope | **Debian 12 + Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 LTS**, amd64, single `.deb` | | A3 | macOS collection source | **osquery**. Endpoint Security framework requires an Apple entitlement, so excluded from v1 and kept as a v2 candidate | | A4 | Code signing infrastructure | Windows **SSL.com EV + eSigner**, Linux **built from scratch**, macOS **new Apple Developer Program enrollment** | | A5 | Giganto SAN verification status | **Not implemented**. Tracked as a separate issue | | A6 | Portal rollout order | **aice-web-next and aimer-web in parallel** | | A7 | Reference implementation OS | **Linux first** with Windows platform-specific work in parallel | | A8 | Closed-network reachability | **Assumed reachable**. Air-gapped environments are out of v1 scope | ### B block — design details **Runtime policy** | # | Item | Decision | |---|---|---| | B1 | Cert lifetime | **24 hours** | | B2 | Renewal trigger | **2/3 of cert lifetime** (≈16h mark) | | B3 | Transient failure retry | Exponential backoff (30s → 5m → 15m → ...), until cert expiry | | B3' | Authoritative denial | **Stop retrying immediately**, stay running until current cert expires | | B4 | Grace period | No separate value (cert lifetime itself is the natural grace window) | **Activation bundle** | # | Item | Decision | |---|---|---| | C1 | Content | EAB credential, responder HMAC (kid + secret), step-ca directory URL, CA root cert, Giganto addr/server_name, agent_name, kind, host_id, portal grant scope reference. **Does not contain the MDM fingerprint or one-time nonce** (those are the second factor held out-of-band) | | C2 | Delivery | Authenticated portal session; **15-minute TTL**; re-download disabled by default, requires explicit "Reissue bundle" which rotates all embedded credentials | | C3 | Format | **JSON** | | C4 | After first use | **Delete** (prevent reuse) | | C5 | Enrollment trust | **Two-factor binding**: either Path A (host identifier from MDM, pre-registered on the host row) or Path B (portal-issued one-time nonce delivered out-of-band to the installing admin). The second factor is carried inside the CSR through a private-OID custom extension that step-ca strips from the issued cert; the authorizing webhook reads it from the CSR and compares to portal state. Path A is **not** cryptographic attestation — see "Wire format" and v2 candidate `device-attest-01` | **Agent behavior** | # | Item | Decision | |---|---|---| | E1 | State machine | `PendingActivation → Enrolling → Running ⇄ Renewing → Suspended → Stopped` | | E2 | Key storage v1 baseline | PEM with per-OS permissions (Windows ACL / Linux 600 / macOS 600). `KeyStore` trait is introduced in Phase 4a-1 so that native backends can be added without agent rewrites | | E2' | Key storage v1 optional | **Windows**: operators may choose `WindowsCertStore` (LocalMachine\\My) or DPAPI-protected PEM from v1. The PEM fallback exists only for environments where the Cert Store is not available. Linux and macOS native backends (kernel keyring, Keychain) are deferred to a later phase | | E3 | Host fingerprint | **Two distinct values, two distinct roles, two distinct phases.** `expected_fingerprint` (Path A only) is **pre-registered by the admin before bundle issuance** and is checked by the authorizing webhook at every finalize — this is an authentication factor (Phase 1). `observed_fingerprint` is recorded **when enrollment is confirmed** (Phase 2 — Giganto reports the first connection), set-once and never overwritten — this is a forensic baseline, not an issuance factor | | E4 | Linux service scope | **System service only**, no user service | | E5 | Failure modes by stage | **No valid bundle at service start** → service stays in `PendingActivation`; the admin re-injects the bundle. **Enrollment attempted, transient failure** (network, timeout) → service retries in `Enrolling` with exponential backoff. **Enrollment attempted, non-transient failure** (authoritative denial, protocol error) → service transitions to `Suspended`. This section defines the additional factors that pin a bundle to the specific host the admin intended. ### Threat model An attacker who obtains a freshly issued bundle (by intercepting a download, exfiltrating it from a share, etc.) could otherwise: 1. Run `reproduce-*` on an attacker-controlled machine. 2. Use the EAB credential and responder HMAC from the bundle to complete ACME enrollment. 3. Receive a valid short-lived certificate. 4. Connect to Giganto and masquerade as the intended host. The bundle's 1-hour TTL shrinks the race window but does not close it. An attacker who is fast enough, or who intercepts the bundle before the legitimate installer runs, can win the race. First-use binding (`E3`) catches the loser after the fact, but by then the attacker already holds a valid identity. ### Defense: portal-pinned host identity The portal requires an **admin-supplied host pre-registration** before issuing a bundle. At least one of the following two paths must be used; both are acceptable for v1, and the portal records which path was chosen for audit. **Path A — MDM-sourced pre-registration (preferred where MDM is in place)** 1. The admin selects the target host from an MDM inventory (Intune, Jamf, Kandji, etc.) inside the portal's "Add host" flow. 2. The portal reads the MDM-provided host identifier: Windows `MachineGuid`, Linux `/etc/machine-id`, or macOS `IOPlatformUUID`. 3. The portal records the value in `host.expected_fingerprint` and binds it to the activation token. 4. The bundle and MSI/pkg/.deb are delivered to the host through the MDM channel, not as a user download. 5. On first enrollment the agent reads the same local identifier and embeds it in the CSR through a custom extension (see "Wire format" below). The authorizing webhook extracts the value and compares it to `host.expected_fingerprint`. A mismatch returns `{"allow": false, "reason": "fingerprint_mismatch"}`. **Important caveat about Path A's strength.** `MachineGuid`, `/etc/machine-id`, and `IOPlatformUUID` are *readable values*, not *cryptographic attestations*. Any process running on the host can read them, and an attacker who at any point had access to the victim host (or to a backup or an inventory dump) can reproduce them. Path A therefore **raises the bar significantly** — an attacker must obtain both the bundle *and* the victim's fingerprint, two values that travel through completely different channels — but it is **not** the same as TPM-rooted device identity. Hardware-rooted attestation via `device-attest-01` + TPM (Windows / Linux) and Secure Enclave (macOS) is tracked as a v2 candidate. **Path B — portal-issued one-time nonce (for sites without MDM)** 1. The admin clicks "Add host" and provides the target hostname and a short description. 2. The portal generates two values: the normal activation bundle **and a short 8-character nonce** displayed only to the admin in the UI. 3. The admin delivers the bundle *and the nonce* to the host via two separate channels (e.g. the bundle via file copy, the nonce via phone, chat, or SMS to the installing operator). 4. The installer prompts for the nonce alongside the bundle path. The agent embeds the nonce in the CSR through a custom extension (see "Wire format" below). 5. The authorizing webhook extracts the nonce and verifies it against `host.expected_nonce_hash` (constant-time comparison against a stored hash). The nonce is single-use and consumed on first successful enrollment. This path requires a live out-of-band channel (phone, chat) but does not require MDM. It reduces the attack surface from "whoever can read the bundle file" to "whoever can read the bundle file AND intercepts the out-of-band nonce". ### Wire format — how the second factor reaches the webhook step-ca's authorizing webhook receives the parsed CSR as JSON. The agent's second-factor value therefore has to live **inside the CSR itself**. We carry it in **custom X.509 extensions under a private OID arc** so that the values are visible to the webhook but can be stripped from the issued certificate by the step-ca template (we do not want fingerprints or nonces baked into long-lived public artifacts). Between the webhook response and the agent's successful cert installation, the following steps can still fail: ``` webhook allow → step-ca signs cert → agent downloads cert → agent stores locally → agent connects to Giganto ↑ can fail (network) ↑ can fail (disk) ``` If `observed_fingerprint` were recorded and the nonce consumed at webhook time, a download failure would leave the enrollment in a broken state: the one-time credentials are gone but the agent never received its cert. This would lock out Path B enrollments. The design therefore uses a **two-phase model**: **Phase 1 — Authorization + scoped enrollment lease (webhook time)** The webhook checks fingerprint, nonce, and host authorization status. **Lease behavior depends on the host's current state:** *Initial enrollment (`host.status = Enrolling`):* If all checks pass and no lease is currently held, the webhook sets a **scoped enrollment lease** on the host row: - `host.pending_issuance_key_hash = SHA-256(CSR public key)` — the lease is bound to a specific CSR key, not to the host as a whole. - `host.pending_since = now()` Subsequent webhook calls for the **same host** are handled as follows: | Subsequent call's CSR key hash | Lease status | Decision | |---|---|---| | Matches `pending_issuance_key_hash` | Lease held | **Allow** (idempotent retry — the agent is re-trying its own enrollment) | | Does not match | Lease held | **Deny** (`enrollment_already_in_progress` — a different key means a different ACME flow, which is the concurrent-issuance attack the lease prevents) | | Any | Lease expired | **Allow** (lease timed out; treat as a fresh attempt, re-set the lease with the new key hash) | The lease timeout is set to the **ACME order lifetime** configured in step-ca (typically 1–4 hours), not the cert lifetime (24 hours). A duplicate renewal cert is a minor concern (two valid certs briefly overlap until the old one expires) and is far less dangerous than a service outage caused by a lease blocking a legitimate retry during the 8-hour renewal window. If a renewal webhook fails after `allow`, the agent simply retries the ACME order or cert download with backoff. Nonce verification is not involved in renewals — `expected_nonce_hash` was already consumed during the original Phase 2 confirmation and is null for any host in `Active` status. The portal subscribes to this subscription over the existing mTLS-authenticated GraphQL connection and receives a notification with `{ agent_name, cert_serial }`. On receiving the event, the portal atomically: 1. Sets `host.cert_serial` to the confirmed serial. 2. Marks `activation_token.used_at`. 5. Clears `host.pending_issuance_key_hash` and `host.pending_since` (enrollment lease released). 6. Transitions `host.status` from `Enrolling` to `Active`. 7. Those are held by the host's hardware or the admin's out-of-band channel. This makes the bundle useless on its own even if intercepted. ### Summary | Factor | Held by | How it is delivered to the agent | How the portal verifies | |---|---|---|---| | EAB credential | activation bundle | bundle file | step-ca consumes on `newAccount` | | Responder HMAC | activation bundle | bundle file | bootroot responder verifies | | Host fingerprint (Path A) | host hardware | read locally by the agent | authorizing webhook compares to `host.expected_fingerprint` | | One-time nonce (Path B) | admin, out-of-band | admin enters during installation | authorizing webhook hashes and compares to `host.expected_nonce_hash` (constant-time, KDF), single-use | A single stolen factor cannot produce a valid cert. Both the bundle **and** either a matching hardware identifier or an intercepted out-of-band nonce are required. --- ## Activation bundle `activation.json` ### Schema ```json { "version": "1", "issued_at": "2026-04-11T14:30:00Z", "expires_at": "2026-04-11T14:45:00Z", "host_id": "01HP5NXQ...", "san_identifier": "01HP5NXQ.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com", "agent_name": "01HP5NXQ", "kind": "sysmon", "grant_scope": { "kind": "environment_customer", "aice_id": "env-prod-kr", "customer_id": "cust-division-a" }, "trust_model": { "second_factor": "mdm_fingerprint" }, "step_ca": { "directory": "https://step-ca.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com/acme/endpoints/directory", "ca_root_pem": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n..." }, "eab": { "kid": "eab_01HP5...", "hmac_b64": "..." }, "responder": { "url": "https://responder.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com", "hmac_kid": "hmac_01HP5...", "hmac_secret_b64": "..." }, "giganto": { "addr": "giganto.aimer.aicers.com:38370", "server_name": "giganto.aimer.aicers.com" } } ``` Note: `trust_model.second_factor` tells the agent which second factor to collect at enrollment time. `"mdm_fingerprint"` = Path A (read local hardware ID), `"nonce"` = Path B (prompt the installing admin). The bundle never contains the actual fingerprint or nonce value. ### Delivery and lifetime - Downloadable only through an authenticated portal session. - TTL of **15 minutes** from issuance. A bundle past its TTL is unusable even if copied elsewhere. - **Re-download is disabled by default.** If the admin needs another copy, they must explicitly click "Reissue bundle", which invalidates the previous bundle and all its credentials (new EAB, new responder HMAC kid, new nonce or re-read MDM fingerprint). - Once the bundle is used for a successful enrollment, the portal marks it as consumed and it cannot be reused. - The agent also deletes the file after a successful enrollment to prevent reuse. - MDM-based deployment: Windows via an MSI property that specifies a **file path** (e.g. `BUNDLE_PATH=C:\path\to\activation.json`), **never the bundle content itself** — command-line arguments appear in Windows Installer logs, Sysmon `ProcessCreate` events, and MDM deployment logs, so passing the raw JSON (which contains EAB and HMAC secrets) on the command line would expose them. Linux via a file placed at `/etc/reproduce/activation.json`. macOS via the pkg payload. In all MDM scenarios, Path A of the enrollment trust model is strongly recommended so that the bundle and the host fingerprint are never in the same channel. ### Security properties - The EAB credential and the responder HMAC are **two distinct credentials** with separate signing contexts, so a compromise of one does not breach the other. - The responder HMAC is **scoped per host**, so it cannot register tokens for any identifier other than the one assigned to that host. - The EAB credential is single-use. After the first ACME `newAccount` call, step-ca retires it. - The bundle **does not contain the second factor** (neither the MDM fingerprint nor the out-of-band nonce). A leaked bundle on its own cannot complete enrollment. See "Enrollment trust model" above. --- ## Enrollment and renewal flow ### First enrollment (sequence) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as reproduce-* participant R as responder participant C as step-ca participant P as portal participant G as Giganto Note over A: startup: parse bundle,
generate key pair A->>C: ① newAccount + EAB A->>C: ② newOrder (identifier: host-id.endpoints.) C-->>A: HTTP-01 challenge + token A->>R: ③ POST /admin/http01
(token + keyAuth, signed with X-Kid) Note over R: scope validation,
store token A->>C: ④ trigger challenge C->>R: GET /.well-known/acme-challenge/token R-->>C: keyAuth A->>C: ⑤ finalize(CSR) C->>P: authorizing webhook (mTLS + HMAC)
POST /api/authz/host P-->>C: {"allow": true} C-->>A: cert + chain Note over A: KeyStore.store(identity),
delete activation.json A->>G: ⑥ connect (mTLS with issued cert) Note over G: verify SAN ↔ agent_name,
check deny list A->>G: event stream starts ``` ### Renewal (at 2/3 of the cert lifetime) - The agent reuses the existing ACME account key to create a new order. - It registers the HTTP-01 challenge token with the responder under the per-host HMAC kid distributed at enrollment. The responder HMAC is not rotated on renewal. - After the challenge succeeds, the agent submits `finalize`. - **Before signing, step-ca calls the portal's authorizing webhook** (see "Authorization webhook" below) to re-check whether the host is still authorized. The webhook receives the requested identifier and returns `{"allow": true}` or `{"allow": false, "reason": "..."}`. - If the webhook allows, step-ca issues the new cert, the agent fetches it, and `KeyStore::rotate()` performs an atomic swap. - If the webhook denies, step-ca rejects the finalize step with an ACME error. The agent receives `EnrollmentError::Denied` and stays in `Running` for as long as the existing cert is still valid. ### Authorization webhook — how step-ca asks the portal The portal is the authoritative source for host authorization; step-ca itself has no knowledge of which hosts are still allowed. The link between the two is a **step-ca `AUTHORIZING` webhook** configured on the `endpoints` provisioner. Flow on every issuance (initial enrollment and every renewal): ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as agent participant C as step-ca participant P as portal A->>C: finalize(CSR, identifier = host-id.endpoints.) Note over C: before signing,
step-ca calls the webhook C->>P: POST /api/authz/host (over mTLS)
X-Smallstep-Signature: HMAC(body)
{ "request": { "identifier": ..., "san": [...], "extensions": [...] } } Note over P: look up host authorization state:
• host.status in {Enrolling, Active}?
• customer / environment within expiry?
• still inside max_hosts? alt host still authorized P-->>C: {"allow": true} C-->>A: new cert + chain else host suspended or revoked P-->>C: {"allow": false, "reason": "host_suspended"} C-->>A: ACME error
(EnrollmentError::Denied on the agent side) end ``` Key properties of the webhook: - **Defense in depth: HMAC plus mTLS**. Step-ca signs every webhook request with a shared secret stored in OpenBao, and the underlying HTTPS transport uses **mTLS between step-ca and the portal** (step-ca presents the certificate issued by its own internal-services provisioner; the portal pins that certificate's issuer). HMAC alone would suffice for authentication, but combining it with mTLS localizes the trust surface: even if the HMAC secret leaks, an attacker still needs a valid client certificate from the internal services CA to reach the endpoint at all. The portal rejects any call that fails either check. - **Stateless from step-ca's side**: step-ca keeps no host allow/deny list of its own. Every decision goes back to the portal, which is the single source of truth. - **Immediate effect**: once the admin flips `host.status` in the portal database, the next webhook invocation (i.e. the next renewal attempt for that host) sees the change. There is no cache or replication delay. - **Audit trail**: every webhook call is logged on both sides — step-ca records the decision, and the portal records who asked (mTLS client identity + HMAC kid), the host identifier, and the decision returned. - **Logging redaction of secret material**: the CSR body contains the host fingerprint (OID `.1.1`) and potentially the enrollment nonce (OID `.1.2`). These are security-sensitive values — the nonce is a one-time credential, and the fingerprint is a stable device identifier that may constitute personal data. **Neither step-ca nor the portal may log the raw CSR body or the raw extension values.** Audit log entries for webhook calls must record only: (a) the host identifier (SAN), (b) a truncated SHA-256 hash of the fingerprint value (first 8 hex characters), (c) `nonce_present: true/false` (never the nonce itself), (d) the decision (`allow`/`deny` + reason). This constraint is explicitly called out in `reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md` and `aice-web-next/specs/authz-webhook.md` as a MUST-level requirement. step-ca's own logging configuration must also be reviewed to ensure that CSR bodies are not emitted at `info` or `debug` log levels in production deployments. ### Suspension / blocking (two-layer defense: server-side block + agent self-suspension) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor Admin participant P as portal participant G as Giganto participant A as reproduce-host-abc participant C as step-ca Admin->>P: click "suspend host-abc" P->>P: host.status = Suspended P->>G: GraphQL mutation addDenyListEntry
{ certSerial: "S", expiresAt: ... } Note over C: next renewal will be denied
via the authorizing webhook Note over G,A: Layer 1 — server-side block G->>G: add S to deny list (until cert NotAfter) G->>A: HOST_DENIED on active connection, then close Note over G: on every new connection attempt,
check cert serial against deny list,
send HOST_DENIED + close on match Note over A: Layer 2 — agent self-suspension A->>A: GigantoDenialReceived
(Running/Renewing → Suspended) A->>A: Collector stopped

waiting for admin intervention ``` **Result:** - Within seconds of the admin click, the host fully stops sending data. - No new events accumulate locally, which prevents privacy and legal issues. - The agent enters a clean `Suspended` state instead of generating an endless retry-failure log. - step-ca denies the next renewal via the authorizing webhook, so the current cert retires naturally on expiry. ### The two layers | Layer | Implementation location | Purpose | Reaction time | |---|---|---|---| | **Layer 1** — deny list | Giganto server | Prevent unauthorized data from **reaching Giganto** | Seconds | | **Layer 2** — self-suspension | `reproduce-*` agent | Prevent the agent from **even attempting to collect or send** while unauthorized | Immediately upon receiving the Giganto denial | With Layer 1 alone, a still-running agent would enter an endless retry loop and waste local CPU, logs, and event queue space. With Layer 2 alone, a modified agent could bypass enforcement entirely. **Both layers are required.** ### Deny list management - Entries are kept only until the cert's NotAfter - Automatic removal after NotAfter (the cert is naturally invalid at that point, so there is no need to remember it) - Giganto keeps the list in memory with disk persistence (restored on restart) - Deny list management via Giganto's **GraphQL API** (mTLS-authenticated, same endpoint as existing queries/mutations): - `mutation addDenyListEntry(certSerial, expiresAt)` — add an entry - `mutation removeDenyListEntry(certSerial)` — remove early - `query denyList` — query the current list (for operations and audit) --- ## Portal design ### aice-web-next — host authorization extension **Schema additions** (in the existing `auth_db` or a new database) ```sql ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN max_hosts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0; We extend it to support a **dual mode**: **Code changes** (bootroot repo) ```rust // existing fn verify_master_hmac(req, master_secret) { ... } // after the extension enum HmacMode { Master(Vec), Scoped(Box), } trait HmacStore: Send + Sync { fn get(&self, kid: &str) -> Option; } struct HmacEntry { secret: Vec, scope_pattern: String, // e.g. "host-abc.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com" expires_at: Option, } fn verify_request(req, mode) { if req.headers.contains("X-Kid") { // Scoped mode: kid lookup → scope check → HMAC verify let kid = req.headers["X-Kid"]; let entry = store.get(kid).ok_or(Unauthorized)?; if !matches_scope(&entry.scope_pattern, &req.body.identifier) { return Err(Forbidden); } verify_hmac(req, &entry.secret) } else { // Master mode: existing behavior verify_hmac(req, master_secret) } } ``` **OpenBao KV layout (new)** ``` secret/bootroot/http01-hmac (existing, internal-services master) secret/endpoints/http01-hmac-store/{kid} (new, per-host endpoint entries) ``` **Admin API** (used by the portal) - `POST /admin/hmac` — create a new entry (generate kid, set scope) - `DELETE /admin/hmac/{kid}` — retire an entry - Auth: OpenBao AppRole, or mTLS **Deployment topology** The topology depends on the environment. *Internet-facing deployments (aimer-web stack): two separate instances from v1* ```yaml # internal services responder — existing, untouched bootroot-http01-responder-internal: image: bootroot-http01-responder environment: - MODE=master - MASTER_HMAC_PATH=secret/bootroot/http01-hmac ports: ["80:80"] networks: [internal] # endpoint responder — new, separate instance for the aimer-web endpoints provisioner bootroot-http01-responder-endpoints: image: bootroot-http01-responder environment: - MODE=scoped - SCOPED_STORE_PATH=secret/endpoints/http01-hmac-store ports: ["80:80"] # behind a distinct DNS name / load balancer networks: [public] ``` The two processes share nothing: separate deploy, separate HMAC store, separate network namespace, separate monitoring. A compromise or bug in the endpoint responder cannot leak master HMAC material, and vice versa. *Closed-network deployments (aice-web-next stack): A-single is allowed* ```yaml bootroot-http01-responder: image: bootroot-http01-responder environment: - MODE=dual - MASTER_HMAC_PATH=secret/bootroot/http01-hmac - SCOPED_STORE_PATH=secret/endpoints/http01-hmac-store ports: ["80:80"] ``` Inside a closed network the internal services responder and the endpoint responder already share a trust zone (both are operated by the same customer admin). Running them as a single dual-mode process reduces operational complexity without widening the blast radius. **The operator may still opt for the two-instance topology** if audit or segmentation requirements demand it; the two choices are configuration-only and can be swapped without a code change. ### Summary of bootroot-side work (one prerequisite issue) - Treating this as "just security logs" would expose the organization to unnecessary regulatory and customer-trust risk. Data governance is therefore a first-class part of this design, not an afterthought. The design addresses five concerns: minimization, redaction, retention, data-subject request handling, and region pinning. Each is scoped to what is realistically deliverable in v1; more advanced controls are noted as v2 candidates. ### Legal and regulatory framing Concrete obligations depend on where the data is collected and where it is stored: - **Korea PIPA**: minimization of collection (Art. 16), purpose limitation (Art. 18), safe handling (Art. 29), destruction after retention period (Art. 21), controls on cross-border transfer (Art. 28-8, 28-9). - **EU GDPR**: lawful basis (Art. 6), minimization and purpose limitation (Art. 5), data subject rights (Art. 15–22), DPIA when systematic monitoring of employees is involved (Art. 35), international transfer mechanisms (Chapter V). - **EU CRA**: technical documentation, support period, vulnerability handling, and risk assessment obligations for products placed on the EU market (effective 2024-12-10, full application 2027-12-11). - **California CCPA/CPRA**: employee data has been in scope since the 2023-01-01 expiry of the employee exemption. - **United States (sectoral)**: HIPAA if any covered health data is captured; GLBA for financial institutions. This design does not attempt to be "PIPA-compliant" or "GDPR-compliant" on its own — compliance is determined by the full deployment context. What it does is provide the technical primitives that a compliant deployment requires: a place to apply minimization, a hook to apply redaction, a knob to set retention, and a path for data-subject requests to reach the data. ### 1. Field minimization (v1 required) Not every Sysmon/Falco/osquery field is sent to Giganto. A per-kind **field allowlist** is maintained in the `reproduce` repo under `configs/field-allowlists/`, one file per `RawEventKind`. Fields not on the allowlist are dropped by the Collector *before* serialization, so they never leave the host. Examples of fields that are explicitly **not** on the default allowlist: - Sysmon `CommandLine` full text (only the executable path is on the list; the full command-line becomes opt-in via `kind: sysmon_full_cmdline`) - Sysmon `User` raw principal name (only a hashed form) - Falco `proc.cmdline`, `fd.name` for user-space paths under `/home` - osquery `processes.cmdline`, `process_open_files.path` under user home directories The allowlist is versioned alongside the code, reviewed by the security team on every change, and shipped as part of the `reproduce-*` binary. Changing the allowlist is a code change, not a runtime config change, so customer operators cannot silently widen the scope. ### 2. Per-tenant redaction (v2 — deferred) In v1, field minimization is handled entirely at the agent side (see §1 above). Giganto receives only the fields that passed the agent-side allowlist and stores them as-is. No Giganto-side redaction is applied. In v2, customers will be able to configure additional redaction rules per tenant (regex masking, allowlist overrides, path shortening) via an `ingest_policy` table managed by the portal and pushed to Giganto. Redaction would be applied at Giganto ingest time, enabling per-customer rules that evolve independently of agent releases. This is deferred to v2 because it requires Giganto to gain per-tenant awareness in its storage layer — a significant structural change to a system that currently stores all events in a shared RocksDB with a single global retention policy. ### 3. Retention (v1 — Giganto's existing global retention; per-tenant retention in v2) Giganto already has a global retention mechanism (`retain_periodically()`, default 100 days, configurable per deployment). In v1, this existing mechanism is used as-is — all events share the same retention period regardless of tenant. Per-tenant retention (different TTLs per customer or environment) is deferred to v2 because Giganto's current RocksDB storage is not partitioned by tenant. Adding per-tenant retention requires either per-tenant column families, a tenant-aware key prefix scheme, or a secondary index — all of which are significant storage-layer changes. For v1 compliance purposes, the global retention period should be set to the **shortest** required by any tenant's policy. Customer DPAs should document the global retention value. ### 4. Data-subject requests (v2 — deferred) PIPA and GDPR both require that individuals can request access to, correction of, or deletion of data about them. Because endpoint telemetry is attributed to *hosts*, not *users*, honoring such a request requires tracing from a user identifier through the events that reference it, which in turn requires Giganto to support per-field querying and targeted deletion — capabilities it does not have today. DSR execution is deferred to v2 in its entirety. When implemented, the design will include: - Exact-match-only search on a whitelisted set of identifier fields - Two-stage workflow with preview before execution - Hard delete by default (GDPR Art. 17 "without undue delay", PIPA Art. 21 "without delay"); quarantine only with an explicit legal-hold override - Export auditing with signed archives - Per-tenant job tracking For v1, the agent-side field allowlist (§1) serves as the primary mitigation: fields most likely to carry personal data (`command_line`, `user`, paths under `/home/`) can be excluded from collection entirely, so that DSR requests against those fields have no matching data in Giganto. If a DSR request arises before v2 is ready, the operator must handle it manually using Giganto's existing data export and RocksDB-level tooling. ### 5. Region pinning and cross-border transfer (v1 required for aimer-web) aimer-web is internet-facing and may collect data from customers in jurisdictions that restrict cross-border transfer (EU, Korea, China, etc.). Each aimer-web Environment has a **region** attribute (`environment.region`), which determines: - Which Giganto instance receives the events (regional Giganto deployment). - Which step-ca instance signs the certificates (regional CA). - Which `bootroot-http01-responder` instance handles the ACME validation. v1 ships with at least one region; additional regions are deployed as customer demand requires. An Environment cannot move across regions without a full re-enrollment of its hosts (consistent with the "portal binding is permanent" principle). aice-web-next is closed-network and all infrastructure lives inside the customer's own environment, so cross-border transfer does not apply by construction — the customer's own PIPA/GDPR obligations determine the placement. #### Metadata centralization — explicit acknowledgement Region pinning above only covers the **event data path** (Sysmon/Falco/osquery telemetry → Giganto). The **portal metadata path** is handled separately and currently centralized: - The portal database (aice-web-next or aimer-web) holds host UUIDs, host display names, customer- or admin-supplied descriptions, audit trails of admin actions, activation token issuance records, DSR job records, and observed/expected fingerprints. - This metadata is **itself personal data** in many jurisdictions: a host display name and an admin description routinely identify a specific employee or device. - In v1, aimer-web's portal database is **centralized**, not regionalized. That means metadata for an EU-region or Korea-region Environment may be stored on infrastructure outside that region. This is a deliberate v1 trade-off, not an oversight. v1 mitigates the risk in three ways: 1. **Field minimization at the portal level.** The portal restricts free-text fields: `host.description` is capped at a short length, and the UI guidance steers admins away from putting personal names in it. The host display name field is similarly restricted. Customer-supplied free text is the smallest possible footprint. 2. **Audit log scrubbing.** Audit log entries record actor account IDs (opaque UUIDs), not personal names, wherever possible. Where a personal name leaks in (for example an admin's display name), the audit row carries it; this is acceptable because admin identities are inside the operating organization, not the customer's data subjects. 3. **Contractual disclosure.** Customer Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) must explicitly state that portal metadata is centralized in the operator's region, list which fields cross borders, and identify the basis for transfer (SCCs, adequacy, etc.). This is a customer-contract obligation that goes hand in hand with the technical setup. A **regional portal database shard** — splitting the portal database itself by region so that metadata for an EU customer never leaves the EU — is a v2 candidate. It is not in v1 because it requires the portal application to become region-aware throughout (login routing, audit aggregation, cross-shard queries), which is a much larger change than the host-authorization scope of this work. aice-web-next is not affected: it runs entirely inside the customer's closed network, so its portal metadata never leaves that network in the first place. ### 6. Audit, DPIA, and customer-facing documentation - **Audit logging (v1)** — changes to the agent-side field allowlist configuration are tracked via code review (the allowlist is versioned in the reproduce repo). In v2, when Giganto gains per-tenant `ingest_policy`, every change to an `ingest_policy` row will be logged in `audit_db` with actor, timestamp, and before/after values. - **DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment)** — deployments that involve systematic monitoring of employees must run a DPIA under GDPR Art. 35. This design does not conduct the DPIA; it provides the documentation, data flows, and configuration surface that the DPIA requires as input. - **Customer-facing privacy documentation** — the default field allowlist and the global retention period are published in customer documentation so that customers can include them in their own privacy notices. Per-tenant redaction capabilities will be documented when available in v2. ### v2 / out of scope - **Giganto per-tenant data governance engine** — per-tenant redaction at ingest time, per-tenant retention TTL, DSR execution engine (search, delete, export). Requires Giganto to gain tenant-aware storage (currently single shared RocksDB with global retention). This is the single largest v2 item. - **Pseudonymization of user identifiers** at ingest (stable hash + separate lookup table) — defers to v2 because it affects detection-rule authoring. - **Field-level encryption at rest** per tenant — v2. - **Automatic detection of new sensitive fields** in future Sysmon/Falco/osquery versions — v2. ### Scope boundary restated This section defines *what reproduce-\* and the portals will do*. It does not: - Determine whether any specific deployment is legally compliant (that is the customer's obligation with their own DPO/legal counsel). - Replace the need for a DPIA or a PIPA privacy impact assessment in the deployments that require them. - Cover contractual issues (data processing agreements, sub-processor lists, customer contracts). What it does guarantee is that the **foundational compliance primitive** is present from v1: **agent-side field minimization** (data that is never collected cannot be a compliance liability) plus Giganto's existing global retention. Per-tenant redaction, per-tenant retention, and DSR execution are v2 items that build on top of this foundation once Giganto gains tenant-aware storage. Region pinning of event data is v1 for aimer-web deployments. --- ## Platform-specific `reproduce-*` implementation ### Common structure Structure shared by all three binaries: - All of them reuse the common-library traits (`EnrollmentClient`, `KeyStore`, `Controller`, `AgentState`). - Each `main.rs` is a thin layer that assembles `load config → initialize KeyStore → run Enrollment (or load existing Identity) → Controller::run`. - Service-manager integration lives in a per-OS adapter (`service.rs`, `systemd.rs`, `launchd.rs`). - Log sinks are per-OS (`tracing-eventlog`, `tracing-journald`, or an `os_log` wrapper). ### reproduce-windows - **Collection**: Sysmon (Operational channel) — EventLogCollector (#797 Phase 3) - **Service**: Windows Service Control Manager (`windows-service` crate) - **Logs**: Windows Event Log (`tracing-eventlog` or ETW) - **Packaging**: MSI via WiX v4 - **Signing**: SSL.com EV + eSigner - **Host fingerprint**: `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid` - **Key storage**: two backends available from v1 — `WindowsCertStore` (LocalMachine\\My, preferred for production) and PEM files with service-account-only ACL (`icacls`, used when the Cert Store is not available). What remains are details that will be resolved naturally during implementation. - **Responder domain naming** — the actual `*.endpoints.` DNS zones for closed-network and internet environments are an operator decision. - **Rust ACME client choice** — `instant-acme` is the leading candidate (pending verification of its EAB support); to be finalized when implementation begins. - **Per-host HMAC kid format** — whether to use a ULID with a prefix or a different scheme is an implementation detail. - **Cert lifetime tuning** — the v1 default is 24 hours, but it can be adjusted to 12h, 48h, or 72h based on operational experience. ### v2 candidates (out of scope, future decisions) - **Hardware-rooted device identity (`device-attest-01` + TPM / Secure Enclave)** — replaces the Path A "stable hardware identifier" approach with cryptographic attestation. Requires that step-ca's open-source `device-attest-01` flow becomes end-to-end usable, and that TPM 2.0 / Secure Enclave is available on the target hosts. Where available, this elevates Path A from "raises the bar" to "cryptographically rooted" and is the proper long-term answer to the bundle-theft threat model. - **macOS Endpoint Security framework collector** — requires entitlement application and a System Extension implementation. - **Linux / macOS native key backends** — kernel keyring, macOS Keychain. Windows Cert Store ships in v1; the others follow. - **Staged CA trust for zero-downtime CA rotation** — Giganto trusts both the old and the new root during a migration window so that a fleet can rotate its CA without per-host reinstall. See "Portal binding is permanent" for context. - **Signed authorization lease for offline renewal** — the portal pre-issues a short-lived signed token (e.g. a JWT with the host's authorization state, valid for N hours) that step-ca can validate locally without calling the webhook. This would allow cert renewals to proceed during brief portal outages, removing the hard portal dependency for renewals noted in the "Partial independence from portal availability" section. - **Advanced data-subject-request workflow** — self-service request intake, automated 30-day deadline tracking, region-scoped execution. - **Pseudonymization at ingest** — stable hash of user identifiers with a separate lookup table. - **Field-level encryption at rest per tenant**. - **Regional portal database shards** — splits the portal metadata store by region so that metadata for an EU or Korea customer never leaves its region. Requires the portal application (login routing, audit aggregation, cross-shard queries) to become region-aware. Pairs with the v1 region-pinning of event data described in "Data governance §5". - **A-double topology for closed-network deployments** — closed-network operators who want audit-level segmentation can move to the same two-instance topology used by internet-facing deployments. - **CRL or OCSP** — only needed if additional cert verifiers appear alongside Giganto. - **Air-gapped deployment** — an offline enrollment protocol plus manual bundle delivery. --- ## References ### Prior discussions / issues - aicers/reproduce#797 — reproduce restructuring + reproduce-windows implementation plan (the source for this work) - aicers/reproduce#812 — Phase 1: `[lib] + [[bin]]` restructuring ✅ - aicers/reproduce#813 — Phase 2: controller/collector commonization ✅ ### External documents - bootroot `ARCHITECTURE.md` — the PKI foundation for this work: - [§5 System Authentication Model](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#5-system-authentication-model) — the existing table of mTLS connections inside the organization;
